source.title: Regularization Matters: Generalization and Optimization of Neural Nets v.s. their Induced Kernel
source.authors: Colin Wei; J. Lee; Qiang Liu; Tengyu Ma

record.file_problem: not stated; full text is present
record.tranche_reason: Reports neural-network results on test error as width changes and regularization changes, using experiments that conceptually address generalization but differ from the versions' specified recipes and measures.
record.gate_note: The paper also states theoretical margin and generalization results; these are not empirical rows. Figure 2 and Figures 3–5 provide plotted results without exact values in the text. The comparison to the NTK in Figures 4–5 is not the fixed random-label setting in the versions.
record.test_reason: R1 and R2 directly measure test error as two-layer networks widen beyond widths achieving zero training error, bearing on V2. Explicit L2 regularization makes this a different recipe from V2's original unregularized experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that explicitly L2-regularized networks can generalize better than the corresponding kernel method and report decreasing test error and increasing margin with width. They also establish max-margin results for weakly regularized global optima and polynomial-time optimization results in an infinite-width setting under stated assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The width experiments use explicit L2 regularization and measure test error and margin across widths; V2 specifies no explicit regularization. The regularization comparison uses synthetic data and compares L2 regularization with none, not dropout.
record.method_sensitivity: The width sweep includes synthetic data and MNIST; the MNIST points use one trial each, while synthetic points average over trials with zero training error. The regularization comparison uses 20 trials.

fits_no_version.finding: Explicit L2 regularization improves test accuracy and normalized margin over unregularized training from the same initialization on the synthetic task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit L2 regularization can improve generalization and normalized margin in the tested synthetic two-layer networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized margin increases with hidden-layer width on synthetic data and MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider explicitly regularized two-layer networks can attain larger normalized margins.

fits_no_version.finding: Section F.2 reports lower classification and regression test error for regularized two-layer networks than for the compared kernel method as sample size grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularized neural networks can generalize better than their corresponding fixed kernel method on the tested synthetic tasks.

record.problems: The width sweep uses a single trial per MNIST plot point, which the authors say makes those experiments noisier. Exact plotted values and uncertainty bars are not stated in the text. The synthetic width result averages only trials where training error reached 0.
record.rows_left_out: No additional empirical rows omitted. Figures 2–5 report plotted values without exact textual numbers; those findings are recorded as figure-only rows where relevant.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting, chance-level random-label test accuracy, and comparison with natural-label generalization.
The unregularized training recipe, downsampled CIFAR-10, and convergence rather than a long fixed training budget. The study does not establish an interpolation-threshold test-error peak.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and sensitivity to optimizer tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout and its effects across data sizes, configurations, and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with other measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The regularized width sweeps support the widening behavior in their tested conditions; they do not verify the original unregularized recipe. That untested recipe is not evidence of a scope limitation. The theoretical improvement of a generalization bound is not itself proof that actual test error decreases. No exact figure values or uncertainty estimates can be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
The width sweep measures test error and margin, but uses explicit regularization; the study does not test the specified unregularized recipe or downsampled CIFAR-10. MNIST is included.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of tuning or weight decay.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout and its effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
